title: Using present continuous and present simple

sections.title: Telling stories and jokes
sections.content:
We often use the present simple and present continuous when telling stories and jokes in informal spoken English to create the impression that events are happening now. This can make them more direct and exciting and hold people's attention:
• She goes up to this man and looks straight into his eyes. He's not wearing his glasses, and he doesn't recognise her ...
• This man's playing golf when a kangaroo bounds up to him, grabs his club and hits his ball about half a mile ...
The main events are usually described in sequence using the present simple and longer background events are described using the present continuous.
In narratives and anecdotes the present simple can be used to highlight an event. Often it is used after past tenses and with a phrase such as suddenly or all of a sudden:
• So last night, I'm waiting for the bus when this man walks up to me and says ...
• I was in the park reading a newspaper, when all of a sudden this dog jumps at me.

sections.title: Live commentaries
sections.content:
We also use the present simple and present continuous in live commentaries (for example, on sports events) when the report takes place at the same time as the action:
• King serves to the left-hand court and Adams makes a wonderful return. She's playing magnificent tennis in this match ...

sections.title: Introducing news
sections.content:
We can use the present simple in phrases such as It says here, I hear, I gather, I see, I understand and They say, (Someone) says, (Someone) tells me to introduce news that we have heard, read, seen (e.g. on television), or been told. We can also use past tenses (e.g. Kevin said, I heard):
• I gather you're worried about Pedro.
• Sophia tells me you're thinking of emigrating.
• Professor Hendriks is at the conference and I hear she's an excellent speaker.

sections.title: News headlines and contents
sections.content:
The present simple is often used in news headlines to talk about events that have recently happened:
• SECOND QUAKE HITS JAPAN
• FIRE BREAKS OUT IN HOTEL ROOM
• SCIENTISTS FIND ICE ON THE MOON
• FOREIGN MINISTER RESIGNS
We can use the present simple to refer to the contents of books, films, newspapers, etc:
• Thompson gives a list of the largest European companies in Chapter 6.
• At the beginning of the book, three men find $4 million in a crashed plane.
• In the film, Loni Baranski takes the role of a private detective.

sections.title: Adverbs and continuous
sections.content:
We can use the present continuous with adverbs such as always, constantly, continually or forever to emphasise that something is done so often that it is characteristic of a person, group or thing. We often use this pattern to indicate disapproval:
• a: I think I'll stay here after all. b: You're constantly changing your mind.
• Jacob is a really kind person. He's always offering to help me with my work.
The past continuous is used in a similar way with these adverbs (e.g. Was Olivia always asking you for money, too?).
We can use the present continuous to describe something we regularly do at a certain time:
• At eight o'clock I'm usually driving to work, so phone me on my mobile.
• Seven o'clock is a bit early. We're generally eating then.

exercises.question: Rodriguez ___ to De Mello, who ___ just over the bar. The home team ___ much more in this half...
exercises.hint: Live commentary: use present simple for quick actions.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: passes / shoots / is attacking
Live commentary: use present simple for quick actions. The present continuous shows that the action is temporary or in progress now. Look for context signals: at the moment, currently, today, or a sense of ongoing change or temporary situation.

exercises.question: A man ___ home late one night after the office Christmas party. His wife ___ for him, and she ___ to him...
options: is arriving / is waiting / is saying
exercises.hint: Story: simple for main event, continuous for background.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: arrives / is waiting / says
Story: simple for main event, continuous for background. The present continuous shows that the action is temporary or in progress now. Look for context signals: at the moment, currently, today, or a sense of ongoing change or temporary situation.

exercises.question: I went to a concert yesterday in the Town Hall. In the middle of it, while the orchestra ___, this man suddenly ___ on his seat and ___ to conduct them.
exercises.hint: Narratives often use present simple to highlight sudden past events.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is playing / stands / starts
Narratives often use present simple to highlight sudden past events. The present continuous shows that the action is temporary or in progress now. Look for context signals: at the moment, currently, today, or a sense of ongoing change or temporary situation.

exercises.question: 'Government gives health service billions' -> I ___ the government's giving the health service a lot more money.
exercises.hint: Introduce news using phrases like 'I see'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: see
In spoken English, 'I see/hear/notice' in the present simple is used to introduce a reaction to news just received. These are not literally ongoing perceptions — they're conversational formulas.

exercises.question: He ___ (work) late tonight — it's a busy period at the office.
exercises.hint: Temporary arrangement around now → present continuous.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is working
The present continuous describes a temporary situation or activity in progress around the present time. 'Tonight' signals a specific temporary event.

exercises.question: 'Vegecorp to sack 1,000 workers.' -> ___ Vegecorp are going to sack 1,000 workers.
exercises.hint: Introduce news using phrases like 'I hear'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: I hear
In spoken English, 'I hear' is used as a formula to introduce news you have just heard or noticed. It uses the present simple even though the hearing refers to the recent past.

exercises.question: 'President Bergman announced a new public holiday on his birthday, August 6th...' -> ___ we're going to have a new public holiday on August 6th.
exercises.hint: Introduce general news using 'They say'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: They say
Introduce general news using 'They say'. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.

exercises.question: Ed: 'Did you hear that Bruno's crashed his car again?' -> Ed ___ Bruno's crashed his car again.
exercises.hint: Use 'X tells me' to report news.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: tells me
In spoken English, 'X tells me' uses the present simple to report news you have recently received. This is called a 'reporting present' and gives immediacy to the information.

exercises.question: Julia: 'I've got a new job.' -> Julia ___ she's got a new job.
exercises.hint: Use 'X tells me' to report news.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: tells me
In spoken English, 'X tells me' uses the present simple to report news you have recently received. This is called a 'reporting present' and gives immediacy to the information.

exercises.question: Water ___ (boil) at 100°C at sea level.
exercises.hint: Scientific fact / permanent truth → present simple.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: boils
The present simple expresses permanent facts and scientific truths. These do not change and are not temporary — the continuous form would be wrong here.

exercises.question: 'A team of researchers claims to have identified a gene...' -> ___ they've identified a gene which causes some people to sleep more than others.
exercises.hint: Use 'I gather' to introduce news.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: I gather
Use 'I gather' to introduce news. When reporting the content of news, announcements, or official statements, use the present simple to introduce the source (The company claims…, Researchers say…). This is the "reporting present" — it gives immediacy to the information.

exercises.question: A: I can't read this. B: You're ___ .
exercises.hint: Expressing annoyance with 'always'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: always complaining about my handwriting
Expressing annoyance with 'always'.

exercises.question: A: Can I borrow €10? B: You're ___ .
exercises.hint: Expressing annoyance with 'forever'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: forever asking me for money
Expressing annoyance with 'forever'.

exercises.question: A: That was a dangerous thing to do. B: You're ___ .
exercises.hint: Expressing annoyance with 'constantly'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: constantly criticising my driving
Expressing annoyance with 'constantly'.

exercises.question: Why ___ (you / taste) the sauce? Is something wrong?
exercises.hint: 'Taste' here = performing the action (action verb) → continuous possible.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: are you tasting
When 'taste' describes a deliberate action (tasting something on purpose), it can be used in the continuous. As a state verb (the food tastes sweet), it cannot.

exercises.question: A: I think I'll stay here after all. B: You're ___ .
exercises.hint: Expressing annoyance with 'continually'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: continually changing your mind
Expressing annoyance with 'continually'.

exercises.question: A: I had a bad day at the office again. B: You're ___ .
exercises.hint: Expressing annoyance with 'forever'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: forever moaning about work
Expressing annoyance with 'forever'.

exercises.question: A: Shall I phone at six? B: No, we usually ___ dinner at that time. (have)
exercises.hint: We're generally doing this at a certain time.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: are having
We're generally doing this at a certain time. The present continuous shows that the action is temporary or in progress now. Look for context signals: at the moment, currently, today, or a sense of ongoing change or temporary situation.

exercises.question: I ___ lamb, thanks. I'm a vegetarian.
exercises.hint: General preference/habit.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: don't have
Repeated or habitual actions use the present simple. The key signals are frequency adverbs: always, usually, often, every day. These describe what happens regularly, not what is happening at this exact moment.

exercises.question: These days, more and more companies ___ (allow) staff to work from home.
exercises.hint: A changing/evolving trend around the present → present continuous.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: are allowing
The present continuous can describe trends and changing situations. 'These days' is a key signal that something is in the process of changing.

exercises.question: Gielman ___ Henry V in the latest production at the Royal Theatre.
exercises.hint: Referring to the role someone takes (like film contents).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: plays
Referring to the role someone takes (like film contents).

exercises.question: They constantly ___ loud music until the early hours of the morning.
exercises.hint: Expressing annoyance at a habit.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: are constantly playing
Expressing annoyance at a habit. Repeated or habitual actions use the present simple, not the continuous.

exercises.question: I normally ___ the children to school at 8:30. Perhaps we could meet at 9:00. (take)
exercises.hint: Doing something regularly at a certain time.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: am normally taking
Doing something regularly at a certain time.

exercises.question: In his recent book, Wall ___ a controversial view of Britain's role in the war.
exercises.hint: Referring to the content of a book.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: takes
When referring to what a book, document, or written work contains, use the present simple — this is called the 'authorial present'. The content of the book does not change.
